title: Misinformation and Readability of Social Media Content on Pediatric Ankyloglossia and Other Oral Ties
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the top posts under #tonguetie, #liptie and #buccaltie on Instagram; every relevant post was scored statement by statement against a 30-point sheet built from clinical practice guidelines and expert consensus, and the share of posts containing misinformation is reported with its denominator (63/71 = 88.7%). Items are judged for accuracy against an external clinical standard, so this is CONTENT, not QUALITY, even though the paper also reports JAMA Benchmark and readability scores.

estimates.country: Account countries reported: US 30 (66.7%), Canada 7 (15.6%), UK 4, Australia 3, Ireland 1; search not restricted by country
estimates.platform: Instagram (called 'an image-based social media platform' in the abstract, named as Instagram in the Introduction and Discussion)
estimates.measure_type: % of top hashtag posts on pediatric oral ties that contained any misinformation
estimates.denominator: 71 unique posts relevant to pediatric tongue, lip or buccal ties, from 68 unique accounts (200 top posts collected, 11 duplicates removed, 118 of the remaining 189 excluded as containing no information relevant to pediatric oral ties)
estimates.definition: A post counted in the numerator if at least one statement in it was marked as misinformation on a 30-point scoring sheet covering embryology, anatomy, epidemiology, symptoms, diagnosis, management, long-term sequelae, lip ties and buccal ties; correct information and misinformation were marked separately and a percentage-of-misinformation score computed per post.
estimates.misinfo_def: No standalone definition; misinformation is operationalised as content contradicting a "30-point scoring sheet based on clinical practice guidelines and expert consensus" designed by three fellowship-trained pediatric otolaryngologist-head and neck surgeons
estimates.page_loc: p. 147, Results, final paragraph; complement also stated in the Abstract and Discussion ('Only 8 of 71 posts (11.3%) contained no misinformation')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 30-point scoring sheet derived from clinical practice guidelines and expert consensus, designed and approved through an iterative process by three fellowship-trained pediatric otolaryngologist-head and neck surgeons, one of them board certified in breastfeeding and lactation medicine. All 71 posts scored by a single reviewer (L.B.); a second reviewer (A.A.) independently scored a random half (n = 35), giving an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.873; the main reviewer's scores were used in the analysis.

estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated because the frame is the platform's 'top posts' ranking (top 100 for #tonguetie, top 50 each for #liptie and #buccaltie), which the authors concede changes frequently and captures one moment in time. Judgement calls: (a) country_norm=Multi-country because the paper enumerates the account nations (US, Canada, UK, Australia, Ireland), but the search was English-language and not country-stratified, so 'Global' is also defensible; (b) population_scope=general_public because the corpus was defined by public hashtags rather than by a professional roster, even though 84.5% of accounts were business/practice accounts and 69% were run by self-identified health care practitioners — an adjudicator preferring to key this field to who produced the content would set 'professional'; (c) breadth=false rather than misleading because the numerator is guideline-discordant factual claims (e.g. tongue ties cause reflux, sleep apnea, colic), not tone or omission. Note the 88.7% denominator is heavily filtered: 118 of 189 unique posts were dropped as containing no relevant information, so the denominator is posts that made substantive claims about oral ties. Minor internal inconsistency: Results give 16 (22.5%) posts from #liptie while the Discussion says #liptie n = 13.

estimates.notes: Stricter dose threshold on the same 71-post denominator as the 88.7% row, so definition_variant=true and the two must not be pooled together. Useful because it shows how little the estimate moves when the criterion goes from 'any misinformation' to 'majority misinformation' (88.7% to 83.1%) in this corpus.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the per-hashtag ≥50% shares in Table 2 (tongue tie 18/22 = 81.8%, lip tie 13/16 = 81.3%, buccal or cheek tie 28/33 = 84.9%) — these are subgroup splits of the same sample by which hashtag retrieved the post, not separate country/platform/measure cells, and the paper's headline is the pooled figure; an adjudicator wanting hashtag-level rows could add them, they are stated verbatim. (2) The IBCLC vs non-IBCLC split (14/21 = 66.7% vs 45/50 = 90.0% with ≥50% misinformation) — a poster-credential subgroup, and the paper's own headline for it is the odds ratio (0.22; 95% CI 0.06-0.81), not the shares. (3) Median misinformation percentages (overall 100%, IQR 75-100; IBCLC 83.3% vs non-IBCLC 100%) — these are medians of a per-post continuous score, not a share of posts, so no row under R8. (4) Topic composition of the misinformation (symptoms 38 [53.5%], lip ties 26 [36.6%], long-term sequelae 18 [25.4%], management 17 [23.9%], buccal ties 11 [15.5%], diagnosis 6 [8.5%], anatomy 5 [7.0%], epidemiology 1 [1.4%]) — what the misinformation was about, not how much there was. (5) JAMA Benchmark Criteria median 3.0, DISCERN (computed for only 14 posts), Flesch-Kincaid, Flesch Reading Ease and SMOG scores — quality and readability scales reported as medians, no share, so no QUALITY row is possible under the 'means only' rule. (6) Account and post descriptors (business/practice 84.5%, HCP-run 69.0%, IBCLC 29.6%, conflict of interest 40.9%, single images 59.2%). (7) '37.9% of parents used a social media platform to search for a surgical condition' is cited from reference 9 and excluded under R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis (STROBE-reported) of Instagram. A de novo account was created to avoid algorithmic personalisation; on 27 March 2023 the top 100 posts under #tonguetie and the top 50 each under #liptie and #buccaltie were collected (200 posts), 11 duplicates removed, and 118 of the remaining 189 excluded as not containing information relevant to pediatric oral ties, leaving 71 posts from 68 accounts. Non-English posts, posts not about tongue/lip/buccal ties, and adult-only content were excluded. No response rate applies. Accuracy scored on a 30-point sheet built from clinical practice guidelines and expert consensus by three fellowship-trained pediatric otolaryngologists; all posts scored by one reviewer, with a second reviewer independently scoring a random 35 posts, ICC = 0.873. Authors' limitations: top posts churn so the sample is a single-moment snapshot, and professions/qualifications were self-reported in account metadata.
